turns.t: Morning, doctor. I'm Tolu, I'm Fiona's support worker, I come in with her to appointments. ~
Welcome, Tolu. Fiona, I'm Dr Marsh. I know you've been referred about your voice. ~
Yes. I'm a teacher, and my voice is going by Wednesday every week.
How long has it been like this?
Four months. It's rough and croaky, and then it gives out in the afternoons.
Is it worse at certain times?
By the end of the school day. By Friday, it's nearly a whisper.
Do you smoke?
Never. I've never smoked.
Tell me about your work.
I teach Year 3, twenty-eight children, in a noisy classroom. I talk all day, and I'm always raising my voice over them.
That fits. What about your health generally?
I have cerebral palsy, which affects my legs, so I use the wheelchair. It's never affected my voice before.
She's very brave. She won't take a day off. ~
Any reflux, acid coming up?
Yes, a bit, and I take omeprazole, 20 mg once a day, for it.
Good. Nurse Beth, could you set up the nasendoscope? ~
Of course, doctor. Fiona, I'll just spray your nose with a numbing spray. It tastes a bit odd. ~
Ugh, yes. ~
All ready, doctor.
Fiona, I'm going to pass the camera through your nose to look at your vocal cords. Breathe normally, and say eeee when I ask. ~
Okay. ~
Say eeee. ~
Eeeeee.
Thank you. That's it, camera's out. ~
What did you see? ~
There are small swellings on both vocal cords, in the middle where they meet.
What does that mean? ~
With the history of heavy voice use, I think these are vocal cord nodules.
Nodules? Is it serious? ~
They're not cancer, they're like calluses, from overuse. The best treatment is voice therapy, not surgery. ~
That's a relief. ~
I'll refer you to the speech and language therapist, who'll teach you ways to use your voice without strain.
How long will that take? ~
They'll write with an appointment, usually within a few weeks. ~
And in the meantime? ~
Drink plenty of water, rest your voice at breaks, and use a microphone in class, if your school can provide one.
I'll ask the head. ~
Avoid shouting and whispering. A normal gentle voice is better. ~
Thank you, doctor. ~
I'll take you out through the side door, it's easier for the chair. ~
